newsitem.title: USA: Maples, noted U.S. forensic anthopologist, dies.
newsitem.headline: Maples, noted U.S. forensic anthopologist, dies.

text.p: William Maples, the forensic anthropologist who helped identify the remains of the last czar of Russia, died on Thursday of a brain tumour at 59, the university where he worked said on Friday.
Maples specialised in forensic human identification and trauma analysis. He often helped law enforcement agencies identify crime and accident victims by studying their skeletal remains.
His most celebrated case was in 1992, when he led scientists who identified the remains of Russia's last czar, Nicholas II, and his family, slain by Bolsheviks in 1918.

In 1991, Maples examined the exhumed remains of President Zachary Taylor. His team determined the 19th century chief executive died from severe indigestion after eating cold cherries and cream, as his own doctors concluded, and had not been murdered with poison.
Maples also once helped identify the remains of conquistador Fransico Pizarro in Peru and analysed the bones of Joseph Merrick -- known as The Elephant Man.

More recently, Maples was called to help identify the fragmented remains of children killed in the crash of a ValuJet airliner in the Everglades in 1996. He identified 11 of 12 child victims, six of them younger than 12 years old.
But most of the 1,000 or so cases he worked on during his career at the University of Florida involved victims of crimes and accidents.
In 1990 he helped investigators reconstruct the crimes of serial killer Danny Rolling, who murdered five college students in three days at the university where Maples taught and kept his lab.
"Dr. Maples was one of the founders of the science of forensic anthropology," said Michael Baden, a forensic pathologist. "He was a wonderful teacher, a wonderful friend and a wonderful family man."

Maples once said he felt destined to study skeletal remains. As a young boy he discussed with a friend opening a tomb to see if a famous person really was buried there. He saw his first autopsy photos in elementary school.

The brain tumour that killed Maples was diagnosed two years ago, according to the university, but he continued to work almost until the end. He is survived by his wife of 38 years, Margaret Kelley Maples; two daughters; six grandchildren; and a brother, Charles Maples.
